points.description: Purpose: both are more efficient broadcasting methods than flooding, aiming to minimise duplicate packets in the network. Equivalent wording earns the mark.

Reverse Path Forwarding mechanism: on receiving a packet from source S via neighbour N, the node forwards it to all neighbours except N only if its unicast routing table shows that the best route to S is via N (i.e. the packet arrived on the reverse shortest path). Otherwise the packet is dropped. Equivalent wording and the same check in a different phrasing earn the mark.

Reverse Path Broadcast mechanism: nodes learn from observed unicast traffic which spanning-tree paths they belong to (e.g. node X is on the path between A and B if it sees unicast packets from A to B or B to A), and forward broadcast packets only on those tree edges, still excluding the incoming neighbour N. Equivalent wording earns the mark; stating only that it uses spanning trees without explaining how the tree edges are learned from unicast traffic earns half.
points.partial_credit: Half marks (0.2) if the answer says RPB forwards only on spanning-tree edges but does not explain how nodes learn those edges from unicast traffic.

rubric.notes: Full marks need the purpose (fewer duplicates than flooding), the RPF rule of forwarding to all neighbours except the incoming one only when the packet arrived on the best route back to the source, and the RPB rule of learning spanning-tree membership from unicast traffic and forwarding only on those tree edges. Partial credit applies only to RPB if the tree-learning step is missing; otherwise a missing or wrong point earns nothing.
